parts.text: Amos, a herdman from Tekoa, announces that the Lord roars from Zion. Damascus is condemned for brutal warfare in Gilead, and Gaza for carrying whole communities captive and handing them to Edom. Fire, defeat, and exile will strike their ruling houses and cities. Their accumulated transgressions will not be overlooked.

Tyrus is condemned for betraying a brotherly covenant and delivering captives to Edom. Edom is charged with relentless hatred and violence against its brother. Ammon’s atrocities against pregnant women in Gilead, committed to enlarge its territory, bring judgment upon Rabbah and captivity for its rulers. Each oracle names a particular offence before announcing the LORD’s response.

chapters.title: Judah and Israel also stand guilty

parts.text: The series of judgments continues with Moab, condemned for burning the bones of Edom’s king. Its rulers will perish amid battle. Judah is then charged with rejecting the LORD’s law and following inherited lies. Fire will reach Jerusalem’s palaces, showing that covenant identity does not exempt wrongdoing from judgment.

Israel is accused of selling the righteous and poor, abusing the vulnerable, sexual corruption, and profiting from injustice around its altars. God recalls defeating the Amorites, bringing Israel from Egypt, and raising prophets and Nazarites. Yet the people silenced the prophets and made Nazarites drink wine. Coming judgment will defeat even the swift, strong, skilled, and courageous.

God addresses the whole family he brought from Egypt, declaring that their special relationship with him makes their iniquities accountable. A series of questions links events with their causes: agreement enables walking together, traps catch birds, and warning trumpets cause fear. As a lion’s roar demands attention, the Lord’s speech compels his prophet to speak.

Foreign witnesses are summoned to observe the oppression and violence stored in Samaria’s palaces. An adversary will surround the land and strip its strength. What remains will resemble the small fragments a shepherd retrieves from a lion. Beth-el’s altars and the wealthy people’s houses will fall together when God visits Israel’s transgressions.

The wealthy oppressors of Samaria are compared to well-fed cattle who demand more drink while crushing the needy. Their comfortable lives will end in humiliating removal. God then exposes the people’s enthusiasm for sacrifices at Beth-el and Gilgal: their public religious activity continues alongside rebellion rather than correcting it.

Famine, withheld rain, ruined crops, pests, disease, warfare, and near destruction have repeatedly warned Israel, yet the people have not returned to the LORD. Each example ends with the same accusation of unrepentance. God therefore tells Israel to prepare to meet him. The chapter closes by naming him as the Creator of mountains and wind, who knows human thoughts and rules the earth.

chapters.title: Seek the Lord and let justice flow

parts.text: Amos laments Israel’s fall and announces devastating losses. God calls the people to seek him and live rather than rely on their sanctuaries. He exposes their hatred of honest correction, oppression of the poor, bribery, and denial of justice. They must hate evil, love good, and establish justice, seeking mercy for the remnant.

Those longing confidently for the day of the Lord are warned that it will bring darkness rather than light. Religious feasts, offerings, and music are rejected while righteousness is absent. God calls for justice and righteousness to flow like an unfailing stream. Their idolatry, extending back into their history, leads to the announcement of captivity beyond Damascus.

chapters.title: Luxury without concern for the nation

parts.text: Amos warns those comfortable in Zion and confident in Samaria. They dismiss the coming disaster while enjoying costly furnishings, fine food, music, wine, and perfumes. Their chief fault is not simply abundance but their refusal to grieve over Joseph’s affliction. Those who lead in luxury will therefore lead the procession into captivity.

God rejects Jacob’s pride and declares that its palaces and cities will be delivered up. Death and destruction will reach households large and small. Justice has been turned bitter, while the people boast in victories as achievements of their own strength. The Lord will raise a nation against them, bringing oppression across the land’s extent.

chapters.title: Visions of judgment and opposition to Amos

parts.text: Amos sees visions of devouring grasshoppers and consuming fire. Each time he pleads that small Jacob cannot survive, and God relents. A third vision shows the Lord with a plumbline: Israel will no longer be spared, its sanctuaries will be ruined, and the house of Jeroboam will face the sword.

Amaziah, priest of Beth-el, accuses Amos of conspiracy and tells him to prophesy in Judah instead. Amos replies that he was a herdman and gatherer of sycomore fruit when the LORD commanded him to speak to Israel. Because Amaziah rejects that word, Amos announces calamity for his household and confirms that Israel will be carried captive from its land.

chapters.title: Ripe for judgment and starved of God’s word

parts.text: A basket of summer fruit signifies that Israel’s end has arrived. Temple songs will turn to wailing. God addresses merchants impatient for holy days to end so they can resume dishonest trading, use false measures, sell inferior grain, and exploit the poor. Their economic practices reveal the guilt beneath their outward observance.

The Lord swears not to forget their deeds. The land will tremble, daylight turn dark, and celebrations become bitter mourning. A further famine will concern hearing the Lord’s words rather than food or water. People will search widely without finding them, and those relying on the false worship of Samaria, Dan, and Beer-sheba will fall without recovery.

chapters.title: No escape from judgment, yet restoration promised

parts.text: Amos sees the Lord commanding destruction at the altar. Neither height, depth, distance, nor captivity can hide the guilty from him. The Creator who governs sea and land watches the sinful kingdom. Yet he will not utterly destroy Jacob: Israel will be sifted among the nations, while sinners who deny the danger face the sword.

God promises to raise David’s fallen tabernacle, repair its breaches, and restore its former condition. Abundance will be so great that harvesting and planting overlap. Israel will return from captivity, rebuild ruined cities, plant vineyards and gardens, and enjoy their fruit. The LORD will plant his people in the land he has given them, never again to be uprooted.
